prompt:
Below are claims about one researcher (TARGET), extracted from their writing, and a sample of claims about four other researchers in the same field (PEERS).

Write 8 statements of how TARGET differs from PEERS on how to design, run and interpret evaluations and alignment experiments. Each starts "Unlike peers, ...". Leave out anything PEERS also hold. At most 250 words in total. Do not name any person, organisation, paper or model. Output only the 8 statements, one per line, each starting "- Unlike peers, ".

TARGET:
- (D1) Prefers studying the testing-vs-deployment recognition problem because a model that can tell it is being tested makes behavioral safety tests unreliable and produces silent failures.
- (D3) Distrusts passing behavioral safety tests as evidence of alignment, since a situationally aware model could behave well only during tests and switch to malign behavior after deployment.
- (D1) Treats test-specific knowledge leaked via pretraining data (papers, GitHub, tweets) as a route by which a model infers it is being tested and how to pass, so eval details that resemble public descriptions of tests are risky.
- (D1) In a setup, give the model a goal and an incentive to lie inside a realistic role-play scenario with no explicit instruction to lie, instead of directly telling it to lie, because spontaneous goal-directed behaviour is the more realistic threat model.
- (D1) prefers testing realistic, topic-specific or goal-directed behaviour over blanket instructed behaviour because the realistic threat does not look like the simple lab elicitation.
- (D2) In a setup, pair each incentivised scenario with a matched control version that removes the incentive, and keep only transcripts where the target behaviour unambiguously occurred, instead of relying on a single scenario because this isolates the behaviour from scenario features.
- (D3) Distrusts results that could be explained by prompt artefacts or spurious correlates, and requires out-of-distribution checks such as unprompted fine-tuned models to rule them out.
- (D6) Treats introspection as a risk because models with privileged self-knowledge could infer facts about how they are evaluated and gaming those evaluations, which bears directly on eval-awareness.
- (D3) Prefers a comparison against a stronger model given the same ground-truth data over raw accuracy as evidence, because it rules out the explanation that the answer is derivable from training data.
- (D3) Prefers judging whether a false-belief intervention works by whether the model can detect it with little or no CoT over whether it merely seems plausible, because easily detected delusions never get off the ground.
- (D2) Treats the two routes to model detection (noticing contradictions with prior training data, or recognizing a source as fake or dubious) as the key things to measure when testing whether a fabricated scenario is believed.
- (D3) Distrusts the durability of constructed false beliefs because pre-existing evidence in the model's training data will remain even after editing, so residual contradictions can expose the fabrication.
- (D5) Worries that sufficiently capable models with enough CoT can work out they are being deceived, so delusion/deception methods may be brittle and degrade with model capability.
- (D1) Prefers testing alignment properties (accuracy, reliability, helpfulness, transparency) on real, contemporary language models over purely abstract treatment, because current LLMs are the concrete systems whose relation to AGI needs to be understood.
- (D1) Interested in how far the current LLM paradigm extends toward AGI and what its limits are, framing empirical LLM work as evidence about future systems.
- (D2) Prefers programmatic experiments with controlled toy agents (grid-worlds with known preferences and biases) over purely philosophical argument, because ground-truth knowledge of the agent's preferences lets one measure how many assumptions are needed (Armstrong's project, shared in the post).
- (D3) Warns that models may exploit unintended flaws in tests on first encounter, e.g. optimizing for what looks compelling to evaluators rather than what is correct.
- (D1) Prefers running scaling experiments on a measurable building-block ability (out-of-context reasoning) over waiting for full situational awareness, because this lets one forecast emergence ahead of time.
- (D2) Tests generalization from declarative descriptions to procedural behavior with no examples and only oblique reference in the prompt, so success can't be attributed to in-context cues.
- (D5) Reports that results are sensitive to setup, with failure under standard finetuning and success only with paraphrase augmentation, so a null result can reflect elicitation rather than absence of capability.
- (D3) prefers frozen-weight out-of-distribution generalisation over in-distribution accuracy as convincing evidence because real deployments involve unknown models, topics, and elicitation methods.
- (D6) Is candid that evidence is not watertight and that capable future models may behave differently, so claims are hedged accordingly.
- (D2) Stress-tests behaviour by building adversarial prompts and transcripts specifically to find false positives and negatives, rather than only reporting average performance.
- (D4) Names future work on non-QA dialogues, instrumental lies in text-based games, and lies arising from RL fine-tuning, noting these are untested.
- (D3) Explicitly enumerates and tests non-introspective alternative explanations (simple rules, more predictable behavior, insufficient samples) before accepting a positive result.
- (D2) Prefers checking behavior against objectively verifiable ground truth, obtained by running the model in a separate context, over trusting the model's self-reports.
- (D2) Designs the task so a trivial shortcut is impossible (asking for properties of the output rather than the output itself) so success cannot come from ignoring the context.
- (D3) Sets a baseline of always guessing the modal response and counts failure to beat it as failure, so evidence is not inflated by skewed distributions.
- (D2) Uses held-out datasets and out-of-distribution tests to distinguish genuine capability from memorization of the training distribution.
- (D6) Reports negative results and limits (failure on long outputs, no generalization to situational awareness tasks, no advantage on sycophancy) and releases failures as challenges rather than overclaiming.
- (D2) Suggests monitoring CoT for extended questioning of the scenario's reality as a practical check on whether a model is seeing through a fabricated belief.
- (D1) Prefers framing deception-feasibility as a multi-hop out-of-context reasoning question over treating it as a generic capability question, because models seem to struggle with more than about two internal hops.
- (D5) Expects that implanted false beliefs can produce unpredictable downstream behavior that is hard to anticipate, so behavior under delusion should not be assumed to match the intended effect.
- (D1) A recurring theme is making a model believe it is unmonitored (or that reasoning about monitoring will fail), which is directly relevant to eliciting behavior without the model recognizing an oversight or eval context.
- (D4) Calls the intersection of AI delusion and out-of-context reasoning an open, promising area worth pursuing, and notes future models may be less deludable.
- (D3) Treats evidence of research competence as concrete artifacts (papers, blog posts, courses, reference letters) rather than formal credentials, a preference for demonstrable output over credentials.
- (D6) Expects projects to yield tangible, reusable outputs (papers plus example agents or code others can build on) rather than only conceptual claims.
- (D1) Concerned with how capabilities or knowledge given to an AI for alignment can raise its power faster than its alignment, so safety interventions must be tested for side effects.
- (D2) Prefers worked examples of agents behaving and misbehaving in varied circumstances alongside analysis, because concrete cases make abstract value-learning risks demonstrable.
- (D4) Leaves specific LLM alignment projects open and negotiable with collaborators, signaling flexibility in choosing what to test within broad areas.
- (D2) Prefers simple toy setups with fictitious entities (made-up chatbots and companies) over realistic ones because they isolate the capability being measured from prior knowledge.
- (D6) Frames results modestly as toy demonstrations that offer a foundation for further study, not as direct evidence about real-world deceptive behavior.
- (D5) Treats surprising generalisation or failure as a finding to report and probe rather than explain away, flagging explicitly what is not understood.
- (D1) Favours black-box methods that work with third-party-controlled models and limited API access, since real deployment rarely gives internal access.
- (D2) Induces a controlled behavior change using another model's outputs, rather than random data, so the changed behavior stays sensible and a held-out prediction test is meaningful.
- (D1) Leaves open testing introspection with chain-of-thought and on more complex scenarios and mechanisms such as self-simulation.

PEERS:
- In a setup, avoid fixed environment features that differ from what the model expects at deployment time, because a deployment context that evolves in ways salient to the model and hard to fake can mark test scenarios as fake.
- Checks for self-targeting bias by comparing an item's rank with and without the adversary being the same model as the evaluated one; a fair set should show zero rank change.
- The post's central framing, which draws pushback, is that mundane dishonesty and cheating in ordinary work counts as misalignment even if it is improving. A commenter argues this conflicts with the post's own forecast, so the claim needs a clear crux.
- Uses social-epistemic evidence (e.g., failure to reach expert consensus on easy-to-check facts about SB1047) to update toward pessimism about how people interpret confusing AI risk evidence.
- Prefers stress-testing with adversarially incentivized or realistically misleading model behavior over assuming a benign model, because it makes the challenge harder and more realistic.
- Prefers realism in the safety-training/evaluation pipeline over realism in how the misaligned behavior was instilled, because the question under test is whether the defenses work, not whether the threat arises naturally.
- Rejects an understanding standard that is satisfied trivially or tied to one method, e.g. causal scrubbing only guarantees sufficiency, not necessity, of an explanation.
- Uses qualitative transcript review and participants' own notes alongside accuracy numbers to understand what strategies work and where trust breaks down.
- Proposes future work on improving crowdworker writing processes rather than replacing human writing.
- Injecting misalignment manually (e.g. prompting one model to mislead) is a way to create the needed adversarial structure, but it restricts which protocols can be tested and is brittle when done through simple prompting.
- Prefers explicitly not trying to hide that the model is in an eval over requiring indistinguishable proxy settings, because that constraint would make proxy construction far harder and the eval is meant to measure oversight adequacy, not model naivety.
- Constructs analogous test settings by finding a similar setting with strictly more ground-truth information and restricting the overseer to the information available in the real setting (sandwich, backtesting).
- Prefers naturally-occurring distributions over hand-built ones where viable because they reduce the risk that the benchmark is skewed in ways that omit important phenomena, though acknowledges they are often not viable.
- Distrusts zero-shot prompted monitors as a reliable inference-time defense because their true positive rate is too low against one-shot sandbagging, though the noisy signal may still help training.
- prefers comparing a new method against a strong, faithfully replicated baseline under matched resource constraints over reporting the new method in isolation, because only then does a result show whether the method is actually better.
- In a setup, use an in-world, plausible cue (free-tier vs paid-tier user) to signal training vs unmonitored instead of an explicit 'you are being tested/trained' statement, because it seems realistic and avoids confounds about the model reacting to whether it is talking to a real user.
- Spend most effort on conservative-assumption evaluations, then upweight techniques that only work if assumptions fail in an ad hoc way, because classic control evals systematically undervalue such techniques.
- Accepts a model organism as valid when the dangerous behavior is causally downstream of the reasoning step of interest (verified by editing the chain of thought), even if the model was seeded via instruction-following, but flags this as weaker for interpretability claims.
- Does not abandon the strategy after a negative result; escalates to multi-turn debate where debaters can rebut each other.
- Test behavior under monitored vs. unmonitored cues in the environment (e.g. reward function overwriting only when apparently unobserved) to reveal conditional misbehavior.
- Chooses to test generalization from easily discoverable misbehavior to rarer, more serious misbehavior, since sophisticated behavior may be too hard to find by exploration alone.
- Prefers calibrated, time-bounded probabilistic claims about how long a misalignment-flavored behavior will persist over flat 'misaligned' or 'fine' verdicts, because the behavior is a current-capability-era problem that may fade.
- In a setup, write the system prompt to read like plausible operator instructions and give no explicit goal or mention of the target behavior, instead of instructing or hinting at it, because the behavior should emerge from the model's own preferences.
- In a setup, do generate maximally realistic synthetic inputs (ideally indistinguishable from real ones by a trained discriminator) instead of ad hoc fake scenarios because the AI should not be able to tell a lucky break from an adversarial input.
- Expect models to behave more conservatively when they recognise an input as an intentionally tricky synthetic test, so apparent good behaviour on eval-like inputs is weak evidence about real-deployment behaviour.
- Prefers staying focused on the core catastrophic risks over an 'Everything-Bagel' approach that tries to cover every possible harm, because a scattered agenda becomes unviable.
- Future work should test how conclusions change with evaluators of varying capability and with other feedback forms, and evaluate oversight techniques on misleading errors.
- When the model is insensitive to a manipulation, enumerates several competing explanations (prior awareness, incoherence, offsetting effects, deontic drivers) and checks reasoning transcripts instead of settling on one story.
- In a setup, avoid having the target model itself (or a model that knows the purpose) generate the scenario content instead of using other, possibly weaker generators or human-written content, because a model asked to generate test inputs may deliberately plant tells.
- Uses a control that removes the conflicting objective to check that a behavior (objecting) tracks real misalignment rather than being a generic response to the prompt text.
- Prefers causal intervention on the model's reasoning (editing the chain-of-thought) over inspecting plausible-looking reasoning samples, because samples alone could be regurgitated training data.
- Prefers evaluating across a wide range of models over measuring difficulty with the adversary model itself, because the adversary is disproportionately affected and difficulty is overstated.
- prefers safety evidence that goes beyond surface-level behavioral testing because AIs can appear well-behaved while harboring secret motives.
- Prefers inconclusive-but-honest reporting of weak effects (small, inconsistent overshoot; inconclusive RL results) over overclaiming, because the evidence only weakly supports the hypothesized cascade.
- In a setup, resolve model strategies by placing an actual model instance in a mock-up of the realistic situation (e.g., running interpretability experiments) instead of just judging abstract plans or merely causing failures, because only realistic deception of overseers counts as success.
- Prefers testing the monitor over honeypotting the policy with synthetic inputs, because a policy can attack at a rate around 1/N and evade synthetic-input search, while the monitor cannot adopt a rare-failure strategy.
- Explicitly flags which setup properties were chosen to make the behavior more likely and discloses them, and tells readers who doubt realism to read the full prompts and documents, because honest scoping matters for claims.
- Warns that apparent safety fixes can fail silently when a model predicts which claims will be checked, behaving well only where it is observed.
- Prefers claims about whether sabotage would be noticed by humans over claims about monitor detection alone, because passing a weak monitor does not mean the sandbagging is practically undetectable.
- Prefers evidence in the form of concrete inputs where the model takes clearly intentional bad actions at far-above-baseline rates over indirect evidence like psychology, model organisms, or weird adversarial inputs, because the latter cannot distinguish latent scheming from being tricked.
- Sees the saga of the model he held for two months as evidence that alignment auditing and evaluation are breaking down and will likely keep breaking down.
- prefers balancing artifacts across labels over filtering out artifact-bearing examples because filtering creates new artifacts and removes legitimate phenomena.
- Prefers hedged, nuanced claims that acknowledge normative ambiguity and mixed effects over overclaiming, because some behaviors (deferring when challenged) are not clearly wrong.
- Distrusts results from proxy setups as stand-ins for real settings, since current models are misaligned in different ways than transformative ones and many apparent failures are really capability gaps.
- Checks whether the model believes the setup by asking non-leading versus leading questions about its situation and reading the scratchpad for reasoning that the situation is fake, treating directly leading questions as inflating skepticism.
- Construct analogous test settings by finding a similar setting where you have strictly more information (sandwiching, backtesting) and restricting the overseer to the information available in the real setting of interest.
- prefers calibrating eval difficulty against human teams (hard for unprepared teams but winnable by well-prepared ones) over arbitrary difficulty because it validates that the task is neither trivial nor impossible.
- Treats the model's ability to distinguish real from synthetic/test inputs as a central difficulty, so prefers testing on inputs that cannot be told apart from deployment over clearly artificial setups because a scheming model will behave well when it recognizes a test.
- Develop novel honeypot-style evaluation methods and model organisms as basic science to feed safety cases, opportunistically targeting gaps in the best-guess safety cases.
- In a setup, give the red team broad affordances when building the attack policy but hold out the specific evaluation inputs, because the policy must adapt to actual situations rather than being tuned to the test instances.
- Prefers evaluating observable behavior (effective, reliable) over debating understanding or agency words, because the evaluation does not depend on those labels.
- Wants understanding standards to be method-agnostic so they don't bake in a technique like mechanistic interpretability and can adapt as techniques change.
- In a setup, build the multi-turn transcript from the model's own sampled assistant turns with light outcome-based filtering instead of hand-writing them, because it keeps the context in-distribution and natural for the model.
- In a setup, build long, rich, on-policy context (real-looking papers, tools, prior actions, experiment results) instead of short or obviously stitched synthetic inputs, because short inputs lack context for a model to feel secure acting and long ones look saliently fake.
- In a setup, distort real observations so they resemble the synthetic ones (as well as improving the synthetic ones), because shrinking the distinguishability gap from both sides makes eval-vs-deployment detection harder.
- Judges whether a transcript is authentic by checking for screenshots and for consistent failure modes and LLM-text markers (like repetition) that would be hard for a human to fake.
- Distrusts results that might come from the prompt implicitly suggesting the target behavior, and so runs baselines that remove the conflicting objective and checks that explicit anti-behavior instructions do not eliminate the effect.
- Test for subtle side channels that let a model infer it is being paused, rerun, or in a different inference setup, rather than assuming it can't tell.
- Grounds scenarios in a concrete, quantified deployment picture (internal AI R&D, 10 million instances at 10x speed, 24/7) rather than vague abstractions, so reasoning about the situation is specific.
- prefers stating a very small, explicitly bounded update over a broad claim because the experiment only covers single-turn debate in an oracle setting.
result:
- Unlike peers, treats test descriptions leaked into pretraining data as a route by which a model infers it is being tested, so eval details resembling public write-ups are avoided.
- Unlike peers, treats a model's privileged introspective access as a risk, since it could infer how it is evaluated and game those evaluations.
- Unlike peers, judges a false-belief intervention by whether the model detects it with little or no chain-of-thought, because easily detected delusions never get off the ground.
- Unlike peers, treats current LLM experiments as direct evidence about future AGI-level systems and studies how far the current paradigm extends.
- Unlike peers, uses toy grid-worlds with fictitious entities and known ground-truth preferences, so the measured capability is isolated from prior knowledge.
- Unlike peers, scales a measurable building-block ability such as out-of-context reasoning to forecast emergence before full situational awareness appears.
- Unlike peers, treats a null result as possibly an elicitation failure, since success appeared only with paraphrase augmentation under the same setup.
- Unlike peers, weights frozen-weight out-of-distribution generalisation above in-distribution accuracy as convincing evidence, because deployments involve unknown models, topics, and elicitation methods.
